# Base image with OpenMPI, Flux, and AWS EFA support for ARM64
FROM ghcr.io/converged-computing/flux-openmpi:ubuntu2204-efa-arm

# Set non-interactive frontend for package installation to prevent prompts
ENV DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive

# Install build dependencies, clone, build, and install LAMMPS
RUN apt-get update && \
    apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    build-essential \
    ca-certificates \
    cmake \
    git \
    gfortran && \
    # Create a temporary source directory for the build
    mkdir -p /opt/src && \
    cd /opt/src && \
    # Clone the latest stable branch of LAMMPS for a production-ready build
    git clone --depth 1 -b stable https://github.com/lammps/lammps.git && \
    cd lammps && \
    mkdir build && \
    cd build && \
    # Configure the build with CMake for a multi-node CPU environment
    # - PKG_REAXFF=on: Enable the ReaxFF package which requires a Fortran compiler
    # - BUILD_MPI=on: Enable MPI support
    # - CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release: Build with optimizations
    # - CMAKE_C_COMPILER=mpicc / CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=mpicxx: Use MPI compiler wrappers for multi-node compatibility
    cmake ../cmake \
    -D PKG_REAXFF=on \
    -D BUILD_MPI=on \
    -D CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
    -D CMAKE_C_COMPILER=mpicc \
    -D CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=mpicxx && \
    # Compile LAMMPS using all available cores
    make -j$(nproc) && \
    # FIX: Copy the executable from the current 'build' directory, not 'src'
    cp lmp /usr/local/bin/ && \
    # Create the working directory for the application
    mkdir -p /opt/lammps-run && \
    # Copy the example files into the new working directory
    cp /opt/src/lammps/examples/reaxff/HNS/* /opt/lammps-run/ && \
    # Clean up the source directory and package cache to reduce final image size
    cd / && \
    rm -rf /opt/src && \
    apt-get clean && \
    rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* && \
    # Verify that the LAMMPS executable is correctly installed and on the PATH
    which lmp

# Set the default working directory for the container
WORKDIR /opt/lammps-run

# Define the default command to provide an interactive shell
CMD ["/bin/bash"]

# This MiniCluster manifest is designed to run a LAMMPS simulation
# using the Flux Operator on an AWS ARM-based CPU instance in Kubernetes.
# It is configured for a single-node execution for testing purposes,
# with the ability to scale up to 4 nodes.
apiVersion: flux-framework.org/v1alpha2
kind: MiniCluster
metadata:
  # The name of the MiniCluster job.
  name: lammps-reax-aws-cpu
  # The namespace where the MiniCluster will be deployed.
  namespace: default
spec:
  # The number of pods (nodes) to start the job with.
  # Set to 1 for the single-node testing requirement.
  size: 1

  # The maximum number of pods the job can scale to.
  # This fulfills the "run on up to 4 nodes" requirement.
  maxSize: 4

  # The main application container that will run the LAMMPS simulation.
  containers:
    - image: ghcr.io/converged-computing/fractale-agent-experiments:lammps-reax
      # The command to be executed by Flux. 'flux run' is prepended by the operator.
      command: lmp -v x 2 -v y 2 -v z 2 -in ./in.reaxff.hns -nocite

      # This container does not start the Flux broker itself.
      launcher: false

      # Ensure the latest version of the image is used for each run.
      imagePullPolicy: Always

      # Resource requests and limits for AWS EFA networking devices.
      # Note: No CPU or memory limits are set, allowing the pod to be 'Burstable'.
      resources:
        limits:
          vpc.amazonaws.com/efa: "1"
        requests:
          vpc.amazonaws.com/efa: "1"

  # Flux-specific configuration.
  flux:
    # Specify the architecture for ARM instances as required.
    arch: "arm"

    container:
      # The Flux sidecar container is disabled. This assumes that the main
      # application container image has a compatible version of Flux installed.
      disable: true

      # The ARM-compatible Flux image. Although the container is disabled,
      # this setting is included to fulfill the explicit instruction.
      image: ghcr.io/converged-computing/flux-view-ubuntu:arm-jammy

  # Logging settings for the Flux Operator.
  logging:
    # Enforce strict logging mode.
    strict: true

  # Set to false to keep pods and logs available for inspection after the job completes.
  cleanup: false

This attempt dramatically increases the problem size on the maximum of 4 nodes to improve the computation-to-communication ratio, aiming for a higher absolute FOM.

The performance jumped from 14.3 to 48.4 katom-step/s when the problem size was significantly increased on 4 nodes. This indicates strong weak-scaling performance and that the system is now well-utilized. Further increases risk diminishing returns or memory exhaustion. This configuration represents a well-optimized state balancing node count and problem size.

context.details:
You MUST use ghcr.io/converged-computing/flux-openmpi:ubuntu2204-efa-arm as a base image. It includes OpenMPI and libfabric provided from the efa installer for AWS and the entire Flux Framework stack.
You MUST compile lammps setting the cxx compiler to mpicxx and the c compiler to mpicc.
Ensure all globbed files from examples/reaxff/HNS from the root of the lammps codebase are in the WORKDIR. Clone the latest branch of LAMMPS. You MUST put lmp on the PATH and run which lmp to ensure success.
You MUST build LAMMPS for a multi-node MPI environment

context.optimize:
You MUST maximize the LAMMPS FOM, *atom steps per second.  It could be Matom or katom.
You MUST parse a result to include the units for katom or Matom.
You MUST choose the largest problem size to maximize FOM. You MAY go up to 4 nodes. 
You MUST make an effort to increase problem size as much as you can.
You MUST set flux.optionFlags to "-o cpu-affinity=per-task"
context.resources: The resource spec you got earlier is for an autoscaling cluster, so the nodes possible are not there. You must add the nodeSelector to use node.kubernetes.io/instance-type m7g.16xlarge with 64 CPU, 256 GiB Memory, ARM (Graviton3). You are limited to up to 4 nodes.
